summary: An island country in the Gulf of Guinea in Africa, made up of São Tomé Island and Príncipe Island; it was once a Portuguese colonial sugar and cocoa plantation colony and became independent in 1975.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: The Portuguese discovered the two uninhabited islands around 1470 and began formal colonization in 1493; the Diocese of São Tomé was established in 1534, and Catholicism penetrated society along with the colonists, missionaries and the plantation system. Most of the islands' inhabitants were African slaves brought there and their descendants, who were baptized as Catholics under Portuguese rule and, blending in African elements, developed religious dramas such as the Tchiloli. Because of nearly five hundred years of colonial history, Catholicism remains the largest religion.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: After independence in 1975 the Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe established a Marxist one-party regime, and multiparty politics was not opened up until 1990; during that period the state pursued secularization and limited the church's influence. Combined with the church's lack of resources and the scarcity of clergy in rural areas, many people who were baptized no longer take part in religious activities, so the share with no religion is quite high.

ranking.name: Other Christianity (New Apostolic Church, etc.)
ranking.description: After democratization in 1990 the constitution guaranteed religious freedom, and the New Apostolic Church and evangelical and charismatic churches from Brazil entered one after another. Using the shared Portuguese language, these churches quickly attracted followers through radio and community gatherings, expanding especially in poor urban areas and raising the share of Christian denominations other than Catholicism.

ranking.name: Seventh-day Adventist Church
ranking.description: The Seventh-day Adventist Church arrived through missionary networks in the Portuguese-speaking world; it stresses observing the Saturday Sabbath, healthy eating and education, and it runs schools and medical services locally. It grew faster after religious liberalization in the 1990s, but its overall scale remains small, with believers mainly in the towns of São Tomé Island.

ranking.name: Assemblies of God
ranking.description: The Assemblies of God is a Pentecostal church characterized by praying in tongues, divine healing and fervent worship, and it was introduced mainly by missionaries from Portuguese-speaking countries such as Brazil. It grew noticeably only after religious freedom was opened in 1990; its believers are mostly young people and city dwellers, and it remains a small, emerging denomination.

religion.background: When São Tomé and Príncipe were discovered by the Portuguese in the late 15th century they were uninhabited; the colonists brought large numbers of African slaves to run sugarcane and later cocoa plantations, and Catholicism thus became the mainstream faith. The Diocese of São Tomé, established in 1534, was one of the earliest Catholic dioceses in Africa. The socialist one-party regime after independence in 1975 pursued secularization; after democratization in 1990 religious freedom opened up, and new denominations such as the evangelical and Pentecostal churches grew rapidly, while a considerable number of people also say they have no religion.

ranking.name: Portuguese
ranking.description: Portuguese has been the language of administration and the church since Portuguese colonization in the late 15th century, and it was kept as the sole official language after independence, used throughout schools, media and government. In the past most inhabitants spoke a local creole at home, but from the late 20th century urbanization and the spread of education gradually made Portuguese the mother tongue of the younger generation, so its share of speakers is far higher than that of other languages.

ranking.name: Cape Verdean Creole
ranking.description: Cape Verdean Creole comes from the Cape Verdean contract laborers recruited in large numbers to work on the cocoa plantations in the first half of the 20th century. After slavery was abolished in 1875 the plantations lacked labor, and with repeated famines in Cape Verde in the 1940s, many people were forced to come to work and settled; their descendants still use this language at home, mainly in plantation communities.

language.history: In the 16th century contact between the Portuguese colonists and African slaves from the Bight of Benin, the Congo and Angola produced Portuguese-based creoles, chiefly Forro, Angolar and Principense. Angolar is said to be the community language formed by escaped slaves in the south of the island. In the 20th century Cape Verdean contract laborers also brought Cape Verdean Creole. After independence Portuguese became dominant in education and the media, and the number of speakers of the indigenous creoles has gradually declined.

ranking.name: Calulu (stew)
ranking.description: Smoked fish or chicken is slowly stewed with okra, eggplant, tomato and a variety of local herbs in palm oil into a thick stew, often served with cassava flour paste or rice.
ranking.history: Calulu blends the culinary traditions of the African slaves brought to the islands with the ingredients of the Portuguese colonists; palm oil and okra both come from West African cuisine. A dish of the same name also appears in Angola and Brazil (where it is called "caruru"), reflecting the historical link of the Portuguese Empire's transport of slaves and crops across both sides of the Atlantic. Because it requires long stewing and more than ten herbs, it is mostly made on weekends, at festivals and at family gatherings, and it is regarded as the national dish of São Tomé.

ranking.name: Chocolate
ranking.description: Made from cocoa beans grown on São Tomé, which local smallholders and artisanal chocolate workshops cultivate organically, with a rich flavor and fruity notes.
ranking.history: In 1819 the Portuguese introduced the cocoa tree from Brazil to Príncipe, and it then spread to São Tomé; in the early 20th century the islands briefly became the world's largest cocoa producer. But the plantations made heavy use of "contract laborers" forcibly recruited from Angola, and in 1909 companies such as Britain's Cadbury announced a boycott because of the "slave cocoa" scandal. After independence in 1975 the plantations were nationalized and output declined; in recent years the industry has shifted to organic fine cocoa, and Italian chocolatier Claudio Corallo and others have set up factories on the islands, making São Tomé chocolate famous again.

ranking.name: Breadfruit
ranking.description: Breadfruit is a large starchy fruit that can be roasted, boiled or fried, with a texture between potato and bread, often served as a staple with fish or stew.
ranking.history: Breadfruit is native to the Pacific islands; in the late 18th century the British transplanted it to the Atlantic region to provide cheap food for slaves in the Caribbean, and it was later also introduced by colonists to islands off West Africa. In São Tomé's hot, humid volcanic soil, breadfruit trees grow extremely luxuriantly, and a single tree can supply large quantities of fruit year-round, making it a cheap staple for plantation workers and ordinary households. Today it remains an important starch on the everyday table, taking the place of rice and bread.

ranking.name: Feijoada (bean stew)
ranking.description: A rich stew of beans slowly cooked with pork, sausage and smoked meat, with a thick, savory broth, often eaten with rice, cassava flour and greens.
ranking.history: Feijoada derives from the bean-and-meat stews of northern Portugal, which in Brazil developed into a national dish of black beans stewed with cuts of pork and spread throughout the Portuguese-speaking world. São Tomé belongs, like Portugal, Brazil and Angola, to the Portuguese-speaking countries, with frequent exchange of people, goods and food, so feijoada has become a common dish at family gatherings. Local versions adjust the beans and meats to what the islands produce and sometimes add palm oil, showing the blend of Portuguese and African cuisine.

ranking.name: Cooking bananas (banana-pão)
ranking.description: Starchy cooking bananas are boiled, roasted or fried with or without the peel, soft and slightly sweet, a regular side dish with fish and stews.
ranking.history: Cooking bananas are native to Southeast Asia and reached Africa more than a thousand years ago, and were then brought by Portuguese navigators to be grown on the islands of the Gulf of Guinea. São Tomé's tropical climate and fertile soil suit growing them in quantity, and together with breadfruit and cassava they formed the basic food of workers in the plantation era. The name "banana-pão" means "bread banana," which shows that it plays the role of a bread-like staple locally, and it can be seen at almost every meal today.
